Traffic Accidents In Los Angeles

Project Report for STAT 303-1 Fall 2025

Author

Sean Casaus

Published

December 9, 2025

Abstract
This report will serve as an analysis of data on traffic incidents in the city of Los Angeles. It seeks to answer questions about what variables are correlated with traffic incidents, and what can be done to reduce them. Findings of the report show that certain days, time of day, and area can all afect the number and fatality of accidents. It also details the demographics of those in car crashes, namely age and sex. This report makes no causal connection, nor does it claim to encompass all factors in traffic accidents, rather it is meant to serve as an analysis of a certain set of data and provide detail as to some of the facrors correlated with accidents.

1) Inspiration

While more of a hobby than a career interest for me, I’ve been interested in the designs on cities for the last ~5 years. A large factor in what motivates changing to design of a city, whether it be creating more public transit or changing traffic lights and number of lanes in streets, is safety. Because of this, I’ve chosen to look at a dataset (courtesy of data.gov) documenting traffic incidents in my home city of Los Angeles. Los Angeles is facmous for its traffic and subpar layout. The most obvious benefit of exploring this data would be creating a safer city in which fewer people are injured in traffic accidents. There are, of course, more complicated benefits to having this data, such as demographic data informing insurance prices.

2) Problem Statements

  1. What areas have the most traffic collisions? Do these locations have anything in common, and how significant are trends in location? Have these statistics changed over the years?
  2. What is the age/sex breakdown for most accidents? What can we learn from this information?
  3. What days of the year are most respresented in the dataset? What do these days have in common? Is time of day a factor?

3) Data

The data is sourced from City of Los Angeles’s public datasets. https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/traffic-collision-data-from-2010-to-present The dataset contains information about 621677 traffic collisions from 2010 to the present. Variables in the dataset give us information on demographics of the victim, where and when excatly the collision occured and the type of location (ex: street, freeway, parking lot) Disregarding ceratin ‘ID’ variables, which are technically numeric, but correspond to a category, there are 4 categorical and 6 numeric variables prior to cleaning. Categorical variables emcompass location, demographics, and type of accident. Numeric variables represent date, time and age. For questions 1 and 3 we are looking at 534353 observations after cleaning. For question 2 we remove a few more observations, resulting in a sample size of 500424 observations. Each of these observations, after expanding, has 18 variables.

4) Stakeholders

Stakeholders of this project fall under two categories. There are those interested in data on collisions to imporve safety: those in charge of city planning and street safety, for example. Knowing when/where accidents happen is the first step to reducing accidents. For instance, if we find that certain days have the most accidents, police departments or traffic control can be higher staffed. The other category are insurance companies, or anyone who would benefit from demographic information. Insurance companies often base rates off of age, location, gender, education, and similar information. Data on demographics is useful for setting these rates.

5) Data Cleaning

a) Cleaning - Question 1

There is very little cleaning that needs to be done for question 1 specifically. This section will cover general changes made for analyzes dataset as a whole for all 3 parts.

  1. Removing Redundant/Unimportant Variables:

For all questions we will drop the following columns since they are either redundant, or give no relevant information: ‘DR Number’,‘Date Reported’, ‘Area ID’, ‘Crime Code’,‘Crime Code Description’, ‘Premise Code’. This is done simply with the .drop() method

  1. Translating MO Codes:

One of the largest goals for our data cleaning will be the creation of new variables using ‘MO Codes’. These codes contain details about the crime report. For example, 3027 indicates a fatal injury [1]. For the purposes of this project, this is important information. Not all codes will be important, but we will create functions to turn codes into a variable. We will simply so this with user defined functions applied across the MO Codes column. These functions will all boil down to ‘if x.contains(code)’ return True, else return False. The 4 codes we will use tell us whether the accident occured at an intersection, whether a fatal injury occured, if a bike was hit by vehicle, and if a pedestrian was hit by a vehicle. MO Codes has missing values, and since we cant impute them realistically based on other variables, we drop null MO Codes, using is.na() == False

  1. Cleaning Time:

The time variable in the orginal dataset is in a tricky format. Essentially, values are ints whose first 2 digits represent hour (0-23), and last 2 digits are minutes. This format is difficult because a) the variable is not continuous (ex: jumping from 1259 to 1300) and b) leading zeroes are neglected (ie: 00:07 would be written as just 7 and 7:09 would be written as 709). We fix this by first adding leading zeroes with a while loop if there are fewer than 4 digits. After we separate into 2 substrings. This could alternatively done using remainder/modulus. For the purposes of our clean dataset, we will have a ‘Minutes’ variable ranging from 0-1339, which represents minutes from midnight. This creates a continuous integer variable for time of day.

b) Cleaning - Question 2

While we didn’t encounter problems for missing values in question 1, we will need to do some imputing for question 2:

  1. Removing Null Values

The first step for cleaning the data for question 2 is removing any values for which we don’t have a specified sex. Since we are analyzing demographics, we will only keep values for ‘Victim Sex’ where we have a significant amount of information. It is important to note that LAPD have a few different ways of denoting sex. There are 6 unique values in the column, however we can only confidently understand 2. It seems that that X represents instances where sex is unknown, however this category may also include those who chose not to report or neither identify as male or female. Since we can’t separate cases with Non-Binary victims and those with no specified gender, we must proceed with just the Male and Female. It seems all other values for sex are typos or similarly not explained. This is a consequence of how LAPD’s data is organized and because of that this question will only answer for data about Men and Women

  1. Cleaning Outlier(s):

When looking at a histogram/value counts of age for reports, 99 is exceptionally high. It is does not have the highest value count, but in comparison to adjacent agee is irregular. While it’s unclear to me exactly why this is the case. I believe that the reason may be that not all age groups are represented (ie: since the lowest value is 10 and highest is 99). It seems anyone over 99 is grouped into 99. For that reason we will throw away values, since they drastically change scale and mean. In the next step we will impute age values and imputation works better without what seems to be a flaw in the how age data is tracked.

  1. Imputing Age:

While all other missing values are in categorical variables, age is categorical, therefore imputable. We will use make estimates based on 2 of the variables with the highest correlations: Whether a pedestrian was hit and time of day. We use numpy to make 2 functions for line og best fit, one for fatal accidents, one for non-fatal accidents. This does center our values around the mean, since no variable has a particularly high correlation. Because of this we will separate the DataFrame with imputed values from the original. For questions where counts are important, we will use non-imputed, for percentage/rate comparisons we will use imputed data Note: While age is continuous by definition, and the age values are floats, we will take the floor for age, since that is how age is reported (ie: since someone one week from turning 30 is still considered 29, we will consider an imputed value of 29.97 as still 29. The original dataset does not give fractional age values, and we will follow that precedent). Overall 58276 values for age are imputed

c) Cleaning - Question 3

Since question 3 focuses on Dates, we will clean our data based on that factor: Similarly to time, dates aren’t in the cleanest format. The ‘Date Occurred’ Variable is a string in MM/DD/YYYY format. To go from the string to variables representing date, we simply write a function that takes substrings and create 3 columns: one for Month, one for Day of Month, and one for year. All 3 are ints, but will be treated more as categories (ie: we wont be creating a correlation constant between number month and fatality rate, since the numbers of the months are largely arbitrary)

6) Data Analysis

a) Analysis 1

6.a.1) Number of Calls by Location:

To start out analysis of locations in the dataset, we will first look at total number of calls for service by area in 2017 [2]. This is from a separate dataset of all LAPD calss ADD SOURCE. We won’t return to this data, but it will be used to set a baseline for which areas have the most incidents overall

Below is a graph of total number of traffic incidents reported from 2010-2025. The numerical details of this graph are not meant to be compared to the graph above, only the shape and order of areas.

The areas that have more traffic reports proportional to overall incidents are Wilshire, Newton, West La, West Valley, Devonshire and Olympic. These areas are all in the more northern parts of the city of Los Angeles. They aren’t exceedingly tightly packed for the most part being more spread out. Hollywood and central have significantly fewer traffic reports than their voerall incidents. These areas are still north, but are more importantly trur downtown areas, and the closest Los Angeles have to a typical city layout. Southeast and Mission are also lower than would be expected, but to a less extreme extent. Southeast is not quite like any of the areas above, and Mission is in the valley. It seems dificult to pin down exactly why they are lower, and may just be lower since certain areas are higher. It seems as though areas that are less dense, require more driving, have higher representation in the traffic collisions dataset. It also seems that areas more resembling traditional, tightly packed cities have fewer proportional reports.

6.a.2) Change Over the Years:

Below is a set of graphs detailing the nuber of traffic incidents per year, per area: (Note: It is unclear to me why numbers spike for all locations in the 3rd year. My best guess is that some change was made in how data was collected that led to the true numbers not being fully reported. The reason the last year is so low is because the dataset was last updated on 3/22/25, meaning less than 1/4th of the year is accounted for. The drop in incidents in 2020 and subsequent years is almost certainly a true reflection of fewer traffic incidents due to Covid and the ensuing rise in remote work)

Areas can largely be split into 2 categories based on the graphs above: areas whose numbers were (for the most part) consistent, and those who grew year after year (disregarding post-covid). The areas most clearly in the latter category are Southeast, Rampart and 77th. These areas don’t follow a particular pattern from the analysis in part 6.a.1, however, they are all on the Eastside of Los Angeles. In contrast, Western and main Downtown areas remained consistent. The reasoning for this is likely complex, however when wondering what factors relate to higher traffic collisions, recognizing relevant areas is important.

6.a.3) Fatality Rates Per Area:

Below is a graph of the percentage of accidents that are fatal for each area. (Note: The range of the Y-axis is not from 0%-100%, rather, the highest value is still barely above 1% fatality)

While differences in the prior sections were minor, we see greater differences here, and in percentage, rather than counts. We are looking at fatality percentage for two reasons. Fatality is important to look at because the worst consequece of accidents is death. There are mass inconveniences, but the number one priority should be reducing death. We are also using fatality as a substitute for ‘severity’, for which there is no specific variable, because there is no way to quantify. The severity of an accident should also beindicative of how much of a problem it is creating for those not involved, as well as those involved. For that reason, we will treat fatality as separate from total counts, but both will be important when it comes to reccomendations. Here what I most want to focs on is that the two lowest fatality rates by a significant amount are Hollywood and Central. Once again, these areas are the most traditional downtown areas. In fact, they have a reputation for being unsafe or ‘rough’ areas. It seems that that reputation comes primarily from being in the actual areas, rather than driving through. However, some of the areas that were higher represented proportionally in part 6.a.1 lie more towards the middlelower end of fatality rates (Wilshire, West LA, Olympic). Lastly, the areas in the valley and in East LA are almost all of the higher end of fatality rate.

6.a.4) Conclusion:

There are two main conclusions from our first question:

  1. Areas with more calls to police stations aren’t always those with the most traffic incidents, but often are. Areas in West LA,and surrounding areas see more trafic incidents proportionally than Downtown LA. There aren’t variables in this dataset that let us make particularly strong connections, especially causal, but it at least seems that the layour of certain areas does have an effect of how many traffic accidents occur.
  2. Not only are certain areas more conducive to accidents, but some are specifically more fatal, an they aren;t all the same. In general, the more Downtown areas, namely Central LA and Hollywood, have a significantly lower fatality percentage. Also, even though the areas in and surrounding West LA seem accident prone based on 6.a.1,they aren’t more fatal. In contrast, parts of East LA and The San Fernando Valley are consistently the highest fatality rates

b) Analysis 2

6.b.1) Overall Number of Accidents by Age and Gender Demographics:

Below is a graph counting the number of victims per age, separaed into Female and Male victims. We are using the original data rather than the imputed data for reasons explained in the cleaning section.

(Note: As we look at demographics, it’s important that we recognize that only one person’s gender and age are tracked. Because of this, we can’t be exceedingly confident as to whose fault the accident is, and will be treating it as if it is equally likely for both drivers/people involved to be the one whose gender is reported. That is to say we are taking these values at face value, we are not going to try to say these statistics reflect fault, only involvement. Our conclusion will not be that a certain group causes more crashes, rather that certain demographics are more ‘involved’ in crashes)

Here we see that the shape of both curves are very similar, with values low before driving age (incidents involving those under driving age are likely either biking or pedestrian accidents) then peaking in early/mid twenties (most likely because many don’t need to drive prior to graduating college, even if they have a license). Values slowly go down overtime. We will not make any causal claims off of this data, but it is safe to say based off of our data that the number of accidents for age groups goes down over time. (Note that this is counting number of incidents, not based on the total population at that age) We can also see (because of the shared y-axis) that the values on the male side are essentially always higher than the female side. The peak for men also comes more towards 30, compared to the peak in the mid-20s for women.

Below is a boxplot, which allows us to make more specific observations on where the majority of the data (percentiles 25-75) falls

Note: From here on out we switch to imputed data, since we are no longer looking at counting statistics, rather rate

This boxplot gives us a better idea of the distribution of victim age. We see that male victims are sligly higher in age based on the 25h, 50th and 75th percentile. This means that the drop that occurs after the mid-twenties is less strong among men, are less immediate. Both medians lie around 40, which makes sense since incidents only really start in the twenties. This tracks with the afformentioned fact that the peak for men is slighly later.

6.b.2) Differences in Fatality by Gender:

Note: As mentioned in 6.a.3, we will be using whether an accident was fatal or not as a marker for its ‘Severity’ Since we don’t have a specific way of quantifying 1-10 how severe an accident was, this is our substitute.

The graph below represents how many fatal accidents Women and Men had respectively

Graph below uses fatality percentage rather than total count

Between the two graphs above we see a dramatic difference in fatality for men and women. Considering our sample size this is not a coincidence and it’s safe to say that men have more fatal accidents than women in Los Angeles

6.b.3) Fatality of Accidents by Age

Below is a graph tracking fatality percentage by age. Here we forgo separating by gender

With the graph above there is less room to generalize fatality to mean severity, since naturally older people are going to have a higher fatality rate. We still do see a small spike in fataliy in earlier years, namely it increases from 10-25, before staying largely consistent, prior to truly spiking as victim age gets past ~50. We can see this data and conclude that past a certain age, life comes to be more at risk, but I don’t feel comfortable concluding that accidents are less severe for younger drivers in general, rather that younger people are going to be more physically resiliant to accidents.

6.b.4) Conclusion:

From our analysis above we can make 2 claims:

  1. Men both get into more accidents and have more fatal accidents than women in Los Angeles. Men also have more accidents at a slightly older age than women.

  2. People tend to have fewer accidents as the grow older, but accidents involcing older people tend to have higher fatality rates

c) Analysis 3

Its clear that the number of incidents changes month to month, and our sample size is big enough that there is likely a reason, but we don’t have eough information to know why. There isn’t a clear trend up or down as the year goes on, rather, months go up and down.

6.c.3) Looking at the Whole Year:

Below is a plot of each month, day combination and the number of traffic incidents. We will also color code by whether a pedestrian was hit or not. The reason for this is more relvant to 6.c.4

As expected, there is variance day to day, and certain weeks have a significant number higher or lower number of incidents. 6.c.4) Comparing the Top 2 Days to Overall Averages:

For this final section we will look specifically at Halloween and November 1st, and compare their times of day and pedestrians hit distribution to the overall numbers. The reason for doing this is to see if my ideas for why Halloween and November 1st have higher numbers are true. My 2 theories are that there are more pedestrians, and people are out later/intoxicated. I can’t test for intoxication, but we can see time of day and whether a pedestrian was hit. If my theories are correct, we should see a higher night numbers for Halloween, and higher midnight/early morning numebrs for November 1st, and a higher rate of pedestrians hit. Below will be (in order) a graph measuring these statistics for the total of the dataset, October 31st (Halloween) and November 1st respectively. As for the rate pedestrians being hit, both November 1st and Halloween have about 1-1.5% more pedestrians hit by rate, which is not exceedingly high as I expected, but still higher than the overall rate

6.c.5) Conclusion:

There is absolutely variation from day to day on how many traffic incidents there are, and these patters tend to be consistent. There are times of year with an abnormally high number of traffic collisions, and an abnormally low number of traffic collisions. These dates are largely self explanatory. Halloween has the most incidents, and Christmas the fewest. Our data also shows that pedestrians are hit at different rates depending on the day, which is valuable information for keeping the streets safe.

7) Recommendations to Stakeholders

a) Recommendations 1

As mentioned before, the primary stakeholders for information about which areas have the most traffic incidents are those looking to better the design of the city. From our analysis above, it seems as though the ‘optimal’ area is one that is tighter packed and functions more like a traditional city. It seems as though taking steps to make other areas more compact would increase safety. This is, of course, easier said than done, and we haven’t dont enough analysis to point to exactly which factors create more safety, but trying to apply elements of the safer areas to those more conducive to traffic accidents should be a good start. Public transportation and more walkability are good starts. It is also likely that lower speed limits in these places contributes to lower fatality, and could be potentially adopted in other areas. Policies like lower speed limits may not be popular, and city projects are expensive, but safety should be a priority of the city, and that includes reducing accidents.

b) Recommendations 2

If we are to apply the logic that higher risk of accident, especially if severe, should result in a higher insurance rate, our data would support that younger people, especially younger men, can be charged more for car insurance. Whether this is exploitative/unethical is not the question this project attempts to answer, but the reality is that insurance companies use this style of data to make decisions about rates. With more information, such as education, we could get deeper into factors that determine insurance rate. Based on the fact that insurance companies reward high academic performance, it’s likely that higher education is correlated with fewer accidents. Alternatively, this information could be used to try to increase safety. If we see that certain demographics are more dangerous drivers (namely younger drivers), we could try to implement better systems to test and educate drivers before being allowed onto the roadI’d say it’s best to first try educating everyone better and see if it does help reduce accidents, or if experience is the only way to become a safer driver.

c) Recommendations 3

Since we know specific days are more and less dangerous, traffic control and sidewalk safety should be a priority on higher traffic days. Particularly, since we know more pedestrians are hit, we could make efforts to keep certain areas very monitered and allow more time than usual for pedestrians to cross streets. This would slow down traffic, and require a lot of people on the job, but both of these are already parts of higher traffic days. It would be slightly inconvenient to have someone at major intersections, but driving on days like Halloween is already slow and inconvenient. I still believe this would be worth higher safety, especially since reducing accidents would result in some speeding up of traffic, maybe even an amount that outweights the slowness of letting pedestrians have more time.

8) Conclusion

From our analyses we can see that there are many factors in accidents, including many that aren’t encompassed in the dataset. That being said, there are certain variables in the dataset that are correlated with more accidents (area, time of day, age of driver etc). None of the problems we can see in the data above are solved by a simple change, but we should absolutely be working to make Los Angeles safer. We know that certain areas and certain days have more accidents. It’s not fair to just pass this off as a fact of living in a city, efforts can and should be made to reduce accidents, and we can start making these changes by looking for the aspects that make certain areas or days safer. We also know who is in the most accidents through our demographic analysis. We should be putting in effort to better educate drivers. It is likely that moving towards these programs could be timely or expensive, but I’d like to think that in the long run, through reducing accidents time and money could be saved. Also human safety should always be more important than bottom line, especially in a city with as much money as Los Angeles.
